title: Parathyroid Disorders
path: Management of Clients with Problems of the Metabolic and Endocrine System
Conditions Affecting the Metabolic and Endocrine Systems

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Parathyroid Glands
headings.content: The parathyroid glands are typically four small, pea-sized endocrine glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland in the neck. Despite their close anatomical relationship to the thyroid, they are entirely separate structures with a distinct function. These glands are primarily responsible for synthesizing, storing, and secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH), which is a crucial peptide hormone regulating calcium and phosphorus homeostasis in the human body. The histological makeup of the parathyroid glands consists mainly of chief cells, which actively synthesize and release PTH, and oxyphil cells, whose exact function remains less clear but increase in number with age. Blood supply to these tiny glands is rich, derived predominantly from the inferior thyroid arteries, ensuring that they can rapidly sense and respond to fluctuations in ionized calcium levels in the extracellular fluid. When serum calcium levels drop, the calcium-sensing receptors on the surface of the chief cells are no longer activated, which rapidly triggers the exocytosis of preformed PTH into the bloodstream. Conversely, high levels of serum calcium suppress this release, preventing hypercalcemia. For nursing students studying endocrine disorders in Nigeria, understanding this delicate feedback loop is foundational for recognizing how imbalances in calcium metabolism lead to systemic pathology. Interruption of the blood supply or accidental removal of these glands during thyroid surgery can lead to acute disruptions in calcium regulation, making precise anatomical knowledge vital for perioperative nursing care.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Calcium Homeostasis
headings.content: Calcium homeostasis is a tightly regulated physiological process involving the parathyroid glands, bones, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) plays the central role in restoring normal serum calcium levels when hypocalcemia occurs. When circulating calcium falls below normal limits, PTH acts directly on bone tissue by stimulating osteoclast activity, which accelerates bone resorption and releases stored calcium and phosphate into the bloodstream. In the kidneys, PTH enhances the reabsorption of calcium from the distal tubules back into the circulation while concurrently inhibiting the reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubules, leading to increased urinary phosphate excretion. Furthermore, PTH stimulates the renal conversion of inactive vitamin D into its active hormonal form, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). Calcitriol then travels to the intestines to significantly increase dietary calcium absorption across the mucosal brush border. Through these integrated mechanisms, PTH effectively elevates serum calcium concentrations. Conversely, when serum calcium levels are elevated, PTH secretion is suppressed, reducing bone resorption and renal calcium conservation while allowing phosphate retention. In clinical practice, imbalances in this system lead to either hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia, both of which profoundly affect neuromuscular excitability and cardiac function. Nursing students must remember that calcium and phosphate have an inverse relationship in many regulatory pathways, meaning that a change in one often precipitates a compensatory or reciprocal change in the other.

headings.title: Hyperparathyroidism: Causes and Types
headings.content: Hyperparathyroidism is a condition characterized by excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia. It is clinically categorized into primary, secondary, and tertiary forms, each with distinct underlying pathophysiological causes. Primary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly caused by a benign parathyroid adenoma (accounting for the vast majority of cases), followed by parathyroid hyperplasia, and rarely, parathyroid carcinoma. In this type, the gland autonomously produces high levels of PTH regardless of serum calcium feedback. Secondary hyperparathyroidism develops as a compensatory response to chronic hypocalcemia, which is most frequently seen in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). In CKD, the failing kidneys cannot activate vitamin D or excrete phosphate, leading to hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia, which chronically stimulates all four parathyroid glands to hypersecrete PTH. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when chronic secondary hyperparathyroidism leads to prolonged, excessive stimulation of the parathyroid glands, causing them to become autonomous and hyperplastic. In tertiary disease, the glands continue to secrete massive amounts of PTH even if the original stimulus, such as renal failure or hypocalcemia, is corrected, often requiring surgical intervention. Recognizing these classifications is essential for Nigerian nurses caring for patients with renal pathologies or endocrine tumors, as management strategies vary drastically depending on the root cause of the hormonal excess.

headings.title: Hypoparathyroidism: Causes and Types
headings.content: Hypoparathyroidism is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by insufficient production or secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH), resulting in hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. The most common cause of hypoparathyroidism is iatrogenic, resulting from the inadvertent removal of, or trauma to, the parathyroid glands during anterior neck surgeries such as total thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, or radical neck dissection for malignancies. Idiopathic hypoparathyroidism is an autoimmune or genetic condition where the parathyroid glands fail to develop or function correctly, sometimes presenting as part of polyglandular autoimmune syndromes. Another recognized cause is hypomagnesemia, which can severely impair both the secretion of PTH and the peripheral tissue response to the hormone, leading to functional hypoparathyroidism that resolves only when magnesium levels are corrected. Pseudohypoparathyroidism, though less common, is a genetic disorder where the parathyroid glands produce adequate PTH, but the target organs (bones and kidneys) exhibit end-organ resistance to the hormone. Patients with hypoparathyroidism experience increased neuromuscular excitability due to the lack of circulating calcium, presenting clinical challenges that require vigilant nursing monitoring. For student nurses, distinguishing between true hormone deficiency and end-organ resistance is a critical clinical competency when reviewing laboratory results and treatment plans.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations of Parathyroid Imbalances
headings.content: The clinical manifestations of parathyroid imbalances directly reflect whether the patient is experiencing hypercalcemia (from hyperparathyroidism) or hypocalcemia (from hypoparathyroidism). Hypercalcemia decreases neuromuscular excitability, leading to the classic mnemonic 'bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.' Patients may present with bone pain and pathological fractures due to excessive bone resorption, renal calculi (kidney stones) from hypercalciuria, gastrointestinal symptoms like anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, and neuropsychiatric disturbances ranging from lethargy and fatigue to depression and confusion. Severe hypercalcemia can cause cardiac dysrhythmias and shortened QT intervals. Conversely, hypocalcemia dramatically increases neuromuscular irritability, presenting with paresthesias (tingling around the mouth and fingertips), muscle cramps, carpopedal spasms, and severe tetany. Nurses must master two crucial physical assessment techniques: Trousseau's sign, elicited by inflating a sphygmomanometer above systolic pressure for three minutes to induce carpal spasm, and Chvostek's sign, elicited by tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear to elicit facial twitching. Laryngospasm and seizures can occur in profound acute hypocalcemia, representing life-threatening emergencies. Cardiovascular manifestations of hypocalcemia include prolonged QT intervals and heart failure. Student nurses must rapidly identify these contrasting clinical pictures to intervene before life-threatening complications develop.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Findings
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation of parathyroid disorders relies heavily on a combination of specific laboratory blood tests, 24-hour urine collections, and advanced radiological imaging. Serum intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) assay is the cornerstone blood test, which must be interpreted alongside concurrent serum calcium, ionized calcium, and phosphorus levels. In primary hyperparathyroidism, laboratory findings typically reveal elevated or inappropriately high-normal serum PTH levels paired with persistent hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, PTH levels are markedly elevated, but serum calcium is low or low-normal, while phosphorus is often high in patients with chronic kidney disease. Conversely, hypoparathyroidism is diagnosed when low serum calcium and high serum phosphate levels are accompanied by inappropriately low or undetectable serum PTH levels. Measurement of serum magnesium and vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is essential to rule out secondary causes of calcium imbalance. When primary hyperparathyroidism is confirmed, localization studies are performed to map abnormal glands prior to surgery; these include technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy, high-resolution neck ultrasonography, and four-dimensional computed tomography (4D-CT). For nursing students, learning to correlate these lab panels with clinical disease states is an essential skill for safe clinical practice and patient advocacy.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of parathyroid disorders depends on whether the patient presents with hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia. For acute, severe hypercalcemia (often seen in hyperparathyroid crisis), immediate medical therapy focuses on rehydration and enhancing calcium excretion. Intravenous normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is infused rapidly to restore intravascular volume and promote renal calcium clearance, followed by loop diuretics like furosemide only after volume repletion is achieved to prevent dehydration. Bisphosphonates (such as zoledronic acid or pamidronate) are administered to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, though their onset of action takes a few days. Calcitonin can be used for rapid, short-term reduction of calcium by inhibiting bone breakdown and increasing renal excretion. In patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease, calcimimetics like cinacalcet are prescribed to increase the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid glands, thereby suppressing PTH secretion. Conversely, the medical management of chronic hypoparathyroidism centers on lifelong oral calcium supplementation and active vitamin D metabolites, such as calcitriol, to maintain safe serum calcium levels and prevent neuromuscular complications. Thiazide diuretics may also be used in hypoparathyroidism to reduce urinary calcium excretion. Nursing students must closely monitor vital signs, intake and output, and lab values when administering these potent medications.

headings.title: Surgical Intervention: Parathyroidectomy
headings.content: Surgical intervention is the definitive curative treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism and is indicated for symptomatic patients, those with end-organ damage (such as osteoporosis or renal stones), and younger individuals meeting specific clinical guidelines. The standard surgical procedure is a parathyroidectomy, which involves the removal of the pathological or hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue. Advances in surgical techniques have shifted the approach from traditional bilateral neck exploration—where all four glands were visualized—to minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP). MIP is performed when preoperative localization studies clearly identify a single solitary adenoma, allowing the surgeon to make a small incision, target only the affected gland, and preserve the remaining healthy parathyroid tissue. During parathyroid surgery, intraoperative rapid PTH monitoring is frequently utilized; because PTH has a very short biological half-life of about 3 to 5 minutes, a drop of greater than 50% in PTH levels 10 minutes after gland excision confirms the successful removal of all hyperfunctioning tissue. Complications of parathyroidectomy include temporary or permanent hypocalcemia (due to 'hungry bone syndrome' where depleted bones rapidly absorb calcium, or inadvertent gland damage), recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leading to hoarseness, and postoperative bleeding or hematoma formation causing airway obstruction. Postoperative nursing vigilance is paramount to safeguard the patient's airway and monitor for signs of acute tetany.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care for patients with parathyroid disorders spans both conservative medical management and critical postoperative recovery following a parathyroidectomy. Postoperatively, the nurse's highest priority is airway maintenance, as the surgical site is in the anterior neck close to the trachea; the nurse must keep emergency equipment, including a tracheostomy tray, suction apparatus, and IV calcium gluconate, immediately accessible at the bedside. Nurses must routinely assess the patient for signs of hypocalcemia and tetany, checking for numbness, tingling, and positive Chvostek's or Trousseau's signs, and monitor voice quality for signs of recurrent laryngeal nerve damage. Wound care involves observing the surgical dressing for abnormal bleeding or swelling and managing postoperative pain. Patient education is vital for long-term health maintenance. For patients discharged after parathyroid surgery or managing chronic hypoparathyroidism, education must cover the adherence to prescribed oral calcium and vitamin D supplement regimens, recognizing signs of both hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia, keeping follow-up appointments for routine serum electrolyte monitoring, and maintaining adequate hydration and mobility to support bone and renal health. For Nigerian nursing students, empowering patients through clear, culturally appropriate communication ensures better compliance and prevents life-threatening metabolic crises.
